criteria.descriptor: Correctly describes HNSW/IVF/DiskANN mechanics and the precise meaning of M, ef_construction, and ef_search (or nlist/nprobe); the quantization families (int8/PQ/binary) and their compression-vs-recall effects; the ~205 GB vs 64 GB memory arithmetic; and pre-filter / post-filter / filtered-traversal semantics. No false claims — e.g. does not say ef_search is a build-time parameter, that raising M lowers memory, that PQ is lossless, or that post-filtering preserves recall for selective filters.

Addresses all four asked sub-parts (index + parameters, memory budget, filtering, verification) and also covers the two-stage rescore step and the filtered-graph connectivity failure mode. Omitting an entire sub-part, the rescore step, or the recall-collapse issue for selective filters loses marks.

Ties each design choice to the specific numeric constraints (205 GB raw vs 64 GB budget, <50 ms p99, ≥0.95 recall, 100-1000x tenant size skew) and articulates the recall/latency/memory trade-offs, rather than merely listing techniques. Explains why partitioning + exact fallback beats a single global strategy given the skew.

Presented as an organized design walkthrough that another engineer in the review could act on: uses vector-search vocabulary precisely, states assumptions, and keeps index/quantization/filtering/verification cleanly separated.

expected_answer_points: Notes that raw float32 storage (≈50M x 1024 x 4 B ≈ 205 GB) far exceeds the 64 GB budget, so quantization or a disk-backed index is mandatory rather than optional

Chooses a graph-based ANN index (HNSW) for the latency/recall target and correctly names the knobs: M and ef_construction at build time, ef_search as the query-time recall-vs-latency dial (or justifies IVF-PQ/DiskANN as alternatives with nlist/nprobe)

Specifies a quantization strategy (int8 scalar, PQ, or binary) with its compression-vs-recall trade-off, AND a two-stage over-fetch + full-precision rescore/rerank to recover recall lost to quantization
Explains that post-filtering collapses recall for selective filters (small tenant may be absent from the global top-k) while a pure exact pre-filter scan is too slow for the 20M-chunk tenants
Proposes tenant partitioning (per-tenant shard/collection or tenant payload index) plus filtered-HNSW for the ACL predicate, with an exact fallback below a cardinality threshold
Identifies the filtered-graph connectivity failure mode (filtering during traversal can disconnect the graph and drop recall) as the reason partitioning the dominant filter matters

Gives an empirical validation plan: build exact brute-force ground truth on representative queries, compute recall@10 vs exact, sweep ef_search to the smallest value meeting ≥0.95, then load-test p99 at that setting
Keeps the distance metric / normalization consistent between the ANN index and the rescore step
common_pitfalls: Recommends plain in-RAM HNSW over full float32 vectors without noticing that 205 GB blows the 64 GB budget, so the design is infeasible as stated
Treats metadata filtering as trivial post-filtering and misses that a selective tenant/ACL filter makes the global top-k return too few (or zero) valid hits, collapsing recall
Names a heavy quantizer (PQ or binary) but forgets the two-stage full-precision rescore, leaving the stated ≥0.95 recall unattainable
Mislabels HNSW parameters — e.g. claims ef_search is set at build time, that larger M reduces memory, or conflates ef_construction with ef_search
'Verifies' recall by eyeballing answer quality or by treating the ANN index's own output as ground truth, instead of comparing against exact brute-force k-NN
Applies one global strategy (always exact scan, or one shared graph for all tenants) that ignores the 100-1000x tenant size skew and fails at one end of the distribution
reference_answer:
Memory first, because it constrains everything. Raw vectors are 50M x 1024 x 4 B ≈ 205 GB — more than 3x the 64 GB budget, and that is before any graph overhead. So keeping full-precision vectors in RAM is off the table; quantization or a disk-backed index is mandatory, not optional.

(a) Index. For <50 ms p99 at high recall I'd default to a graph index (HNSW): traversal gives sublinear query cost and strong recall. The knobs: M (graph degree) and ef_construction control build-time graph quality and memory; ef_search is the query-time dial that trades recall for latency. I'd raise ef_search until recall@10 ≥ 0.95, then confirm p99 is still <50 ms. IVF-PQ (nlist/nprobe) is a lower-memory alternative but usually gives worse recall-vs-latency at this scale; DiskANN/Vamana is the fallback if even quantized vectors won't fit in RAM, since it keeps compressed vectors in RAM and full vectors on SSD.

(b) Memory budget. Use quantization plus two-stage retrieval. Scalar int8 quantization is ~4x (≈51 GB) with small recall loss; product quantization (PQ) or binary quantization compress far more but distances become approximate, so recall drops. Recover it with over-fetch + rescore: the compressed index returns a shortlist (e.g. top 100-200), then those candidates are re-scored against full-precision vectors (held on SSD or a rescore store) to produce the final top-10. Binary/PQ shortlist + int8/full rescore is the standard way to hit an aggressive RAM budget while preserving recall.

(c) Filtering — the crux. Naive post-filtering (global ANN top-k, then drop rows failing tenant/ACL) collapses recall for selective filters: a small tenant's few hundred docs may not appear in the global top-k at all, so you return too few or must over-fetch enormously. Pure pre-filtering (exact scan over the filtered subset) is correct and cheap for the thousands of tiny tenants but O(N) and too slow for the 20M-chunk tenants. So: (1) partition by tenant — a tenant-keyed payload index or per-tenant shard/collection — so each query searches only its tenant's vectors and the graph stays connected within the tenant; (2) within a tenant apply the ACL predicate during graph traversal (filtered/filterable HNSW as in Qdrant/Weaviate/pgvector), with an exact fallback when the filtered cardinality is below a threshold. The failure mode to guard against is that filtering during traversal can disconnect the graph — if too many neighbours are filtered out, the walk stalls and recall tanks — which is exactly why making the dominant filter (tenant) a partition rather than a per-node predicate matters, and why the small-cardinality exact fallback exists.

(d) Verification. Build ground truth by running exact brute-force k-NN over a representative query sample (spanning large- and small-tenant queries and restrictive ACLs), compute recall@10 = |approx ∩ exact| / 10 averaged over queries, and sweep ef_search (and over-fetch depth / nprobe) to the smallest value meeting ≥0.95. Then load-test p99 at production concurrency at that setting; if recall and p99 can't hold together, trade memory (lighter quantization, higher M) for headroom. Re-measure after any embedding-model or data change, and monitor p99 plus periodic exact spot-checks in production. Finally, keep the distance metric consistent (cosine / normalized dot) between the ANN index and the rescore step, or the rerank silently reorders wrongly.
